relevant.sermon_title: Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 9

relevant.reason: Promises the anxious that God knows their needs and gives a sure way to be supplied: seek his kingdom first.

relevant.sermon_title: Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 9
relevant.quote: This care God hath taken upon himself: Cast you all your care upon Him. He knoweth your wants; and whatsoever is lacking he will not fail to supply.

relevant.sermon_title: Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 9

query: How can I know that I am really a child of God? What did Wesley teach about the assurance of salvation?

relevant.sermon_title: THE WITNESS OF THE SPIRIT, Discourse I
relevant.quote: The testimony of the Spirit is an inward impression on the soul, whereby the Spirit of God directly witnesses to my spirit, that I am a child of God; that Jesus Christ hath loved me, and given himself for me; and that all my sins are blotted out, and I, even I, am reconciled to God.

relevant.sermon_title: The Witness of the Spirit, Discourse II
relevant.quote: To secure us from all delusion, God gives us two witnesses that we are his children.

relevant.sermon_title: THE WITNESS OF THE SPIRIT, Discourse I
relevant.quote: every man applying those scriptural marks to himself, may know whether he is a child of God.
relevant.reason: Answers 'how can I know': apply Scripture's marks of God's children to yourself and draw the conclusion.

relevant.sermon_title: THE WITNESS OF THE SPIRIT, Discourse I
relevant.quote: By the same immediate consciousness, you will know if your soul is alive to God; if you are saved from the pain of proud wrath, and have the ease of a meek and quiet spirit. By the same means you cannot but perceive if you love, rejoice, and delight in God.
relevant.reason: Explains how a believer knows he has the marks: by immediate inner consciousness, as we know we are alive.

relevant.sermon_title: THE WITNESS OF THE SPIRIT, Discourse I
relevant.quote: We know that we love God and keep his commandments; and "hereby also we know that we are of God." This is that testimony of our own spirit, which, so long as we continue to love God and keep his commandments, continues joined with the testimony of God's Spirit
relevant.reason: Describes the joint witness of God's Spirit and our own spirit by which we know we are God's children.

relevant.sermon_title: THE WITNESS OF THE SPIRIT, Discourse I
relevant.quote: But I thus love, delight, and rejoice in God; Therefore, I am a child of God: -- Then a Christian can in no wise doubt of his being a child of God.
relevant.reason: Gives the reasoning by which a believer can be sure he is a child of God without doubt.

relevant.sermon_title: THE WITNESS OF THE SPIRIT, Discourse I
relevant.quote: the Spirit of God does give a believer such a testimony of his adoption that while it is present to the soul, he can no more doubt the reality of his sonship, than he can doubt of the shining of the sun
relevant.reason: Affirms that God's Spirit gives believers a testimony of adoption that removes doubt, the heart of Wesley's assurance.

relevant.sermon_title: THE WITNESS OF THE SPIRIT, Discourse I
relevant.quote: By the fruits which he hath wrought in your spirit, you shall know the testimony of the Spirit of God. Hereby you shall know, that you are in no delusion, that you have not deceived your own soul.
relevant.reason: Tells the asker how to be sure their assurance is real and not self-deception: look for the Spirit's fruits.

relevant.sermon_title: The Witness of the Spirit, Discourse II
relevant.quote: The word of God says, every one who has the fruit of the Spirit is a child of God; experience, or inward consciousness, tells me, that I have the fruit of the Spirit; and hence I rationally conclude, "Therefore I am a child of God."
relevant.reason: Lays out the indirect witness: Scripture plus inner experience lets one conclude 'I am a child of God.'

relevant.quote: And it is certain, this faith necessarily implies an assurance (which is here only another word for evidence, it being hard to tell the difference between them) that Christ loved me, and gave Himself for me.
relevant.reason: Teaches that saving faith itself carries assurance that Christ loved me; core of Wesley's doctrine of assurance.

relevant.quote: It might have been said, (and it is all that can be said with propriety,) "Hitherto you are only a servant, you are not a child of God. You have already great reason to praise God that he has called you to his honourable service. Fear not.
relevant.reason: Pastoral word to one lacking assurance: not condemned, a servant of God, to keep seeking and not fear.

relevant.quote: Thus, the faith of a child is, properly and directly, a divine conviction, whereby every child of God is enabled to testify, "The life that I now live, I live by faith the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me."
relevant.reason: Defines the faith of a child of God as a divine conviction of Christ's personal love, witnessed by the Spirit.

relevant.quote: And it does indeed imply a full assurance that all your past sins are forgiven, and that you are now a child of God. But it does not necessarily imply a full assurance of our future perseverance.
relevant.reason: Clarifies what assurance covers: present sonship and forgiven sins, not necessarily future perseverance.

relevant.sermon_title: The Marks of the New Birth
relevant.quote: The question is not, what you was made in baptism; (do not evade;) but, What are you now? Is the Spirit of adoption now in your heart? To your own heart let the appeal be made.
relevant.reason: Direct self-examination for the asker: are you a child of God now, by the Spirit of adoption in your heart.

relevant.quote: If he inject doubts whether you are a child of God, or fears lest you should not endure to the end; "take to you for a helmet the hope of salvation."
relevant.reason: Counsel for someone troubled by doubts whether they are God's child: hold fast the hope of salvation.

relevant.reason: Describes the Spirit's direct witness: an inner calm in which the believer is clearly satisfied his sins are forgiven.

query: Is it wrong for a Christian to try to earn more money? What did Wesley say about making a living?

relevant.reason: Sets the limit on earning: no work requiring cheating or lying, whatever it pays.

relevant.quote: We cannot, consistent with brotherly love, sell our goods below the market price; we cannot study to ruin our neighbour's trade, in order to advance our own
relevant.reason: Speaks to getting ahead: we may not advance ourselves by hurting a neighbour's business.

relevant.quote: it is the bounden duty of all who are engaged in worldly business to observe that first and great rule of Christian wisdom with respect to money, "Gain all you can." Gain all you can by honest industry. Use all possible diligence in your calling.
relevant.reason: Says hard, honest work to earn is a Christian duty, not something to avoid.

relevant.quote: he placed you here not as a proprietor, but a steward: As such he entrusted you, for a season, with goods of various kinds; but the sole property of these still rests in him

relevant.quote: They gain all they can, honestly and conscientiously. They save all they can, by cutting off all needless expense; by adding frugality to diligence. And so far all is right. This is the duty of every one that fears God.

relevant.quote: It is allowed, (1.) That we are to provide necessaries and conveniences for those of our own household: (2.) That men in business are to lay up as much as is necessary for the carrying on of that business

relevant.reason: Sharp warning against aiming at more once needs are met, tied to Christ's command not to lay up treasure.

relevant.sermon_title: Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 9
relevant.quote: It is the will of God, that every man should labour to eat his own bread; yea, and that every man should provide for his own, for them of his own household.
relevant.reason: Affirms that working to support oneself and family is God's will.

relevant.quote: They gain all they can, honestly and conscientiously. They save all they can, by cutting off all needless expense; by adding frugality to diligence. And so far all is right. This is the duty of every one that fears God.
relevant.reason: Says honest diligent earning is right and a duty, but warns it must go with giving.

relevant.quote: It is allowed, (1.) That we are to provide necessaries and conveniences for those of our own household: (2.) That men in business are to lay up as much as is necessary for the carrying on of that business
relevant.reason: Spells out what earning and saving is allowed, and where accumulating beyond it is forbidden.

relevant.quote: Lay, each of you, your hand to your heart, and seriously inquire, "Am I of that number? Am I labouring, not only for what I want, but for more than I want?"
relevant.reason: Gives the asker a direct heart-test for wanting a bigger paycheck: labouring for more than you need.

relevant.quote: it is impossible that an idle man can be a good man, -- sloth being inconsistent with religion. But with what view? For what end do you undertake and follow your worldly business?
relevant.reason: Affirms diligent work and asks the key question of motive: why do you pursue your business?

relevant.quote: Thirdly, this being done, fix your purpose, to "gain no more." I charge you in the name of God, do not increase your substance! As it comes daily or yearly, so let it go
relevant.reason: Direct counsel once family needs are met: do not aim to increase wealth; let surplus go out.

relevant.sermon_title: Causes of the Inefficacy of Christianity
relevant.quote: I call God to record upon my soul, that I advise no more than I practise. I do, blessed be God, gain, and save, and give all I can.
relevant.reason: Wesley's own practice as model: earn, save, and give all you can.

relevant.sermon_title: On the Danger of Increasing Riches
relevant.quote: But if the danger of barely having them is so great, how much greater is the danger of increasing them! This danger is great even to those who receive what is transmitted to them by their forefathers; but it is abundantly greater to those who acquire them by their skill and industry.
relevant.reason: Warns that growing wealth by one's own skill and work carries special spiritual danger.

relevant.quote: Are ye poor? Then you have particular reason to work with your hands, that you may provide for your own household. Nor when you have done this have you done all; for then you are to labour that you may give to him that needeth
relevant.reason: Gives the purpose of working: provide for your household, then labour further to give to the needy.

query: Can a Christian be wealthy without it hurting their soul? What did Wesley say about the danger of riches?

relevant.quote: They that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful desires, which drown men in destruction and perdition.
How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God! It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God

relevant.sermon_title: Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 8
relevant.quote: For a man may possibly be rich, without any fault of his, by an overruling Providence, preventing his own choice: But he affirms it of hoi boulomenoi plourein, those who desire or seek to be rich.
relevant.reason: Distinguishes having riches, which may be no fault, from desiring them, which destroys the soul.

relevant.quote: Not that money is an evil of itself: It is applicable to good as well as bad purposes. But, nevertheless, it is an undoubted truth, that "the love of money is the root of all evil;" and also, that the possession of riches naturally breeds the love of them.
relevant.reason: Explains the danger: money is not evil, but possessing riches naturally breeds the love of them.

relevant.quote: And yet I have not known threescore rich persons, perhaps not half the number, during threescore years, who, as far as I can judge, were not less holy than they would have been had they been poor.
relevant.reason: Wesley's long observation that riches nearly always made people less holy; defines rich as having something over.

relevant.quote: But they do not give all they can; without which they must needs grow more and more earthly-minded. Their affections will cleave to the dust more and more; and they will have less and less communion with God. Is not this your case?
relevant.reason: Shows how surplus hurts the soul when not given away: more earthly-minded, less communion with God.

relevant.quote: But to lay up any more, when this is done, is what our Lord has flatly forbidden. When it is calmly and deliberately done, it is a clear proof of our desiring to be rich.
relevant.reason: Answers the person with more than they need: providing for family is allowed, hoarding the surplus is forbidden.

relevant.quote: Riches, either desired or possessed, naturally lead to some or other of these foolish and hurtful desires; and by affording the means of gratifying them all, naturally tend to increase them.
relevant.reason: Explains how wealth harms the soul: it feeds and multiplies foolish, hurtful desires and evil tempers.

relevant.quote: I answer, It is possible. You may gain all you can without hurting either your soul or body; you may save all you can, by carefully avoiding every needless expense; and yet never lay up treasures on earth
relevant.reason: Directly answers whether one can prosper without spiritual harm: yes, by never hoarding the surplus.

relevant.quote: But the Apostle does not fix the charge, barely on possessing any quantity of goods, but on possessing more than we employ according to the will of the Donor.
relevant.reason: Clarifies that wealth itself is not the sin; keeping more than one uses as God wills is.

relevant.quote: Herein, my brethren, let you that are rich, be even as I am. Do you that possess more than food and raiment ask: "What shall we do? Shall we throw into the sea what God hath given us?" God forbid that you should! It is an excellent talent
relevant.reason: Direct counsel to those with more than they need: do not throw it away; use it as a talent for God.

relevant.quote: Have you the same vehement desire as you formerly had, of "going on unto perfection?" Have they not hurt you by weakening your faith?
relevant.reason: Self-examination for the prosperous: have riches already weakened your hunger for God and your faith?

relevant.quote: Or if you take faith, in the proper Christian sense, as a divine confidence in a pardoning God; what a deadly, what an almost insuperable, hinderance to this faith are riches!
relevant.reason: Names a specific spiritual harm of wealth: it hinders humble faith in a pardoning God.

relevant.quote: Riches are equally a hinderance to the loving our neighbour as ourselves; that is, to the loving all mankind as Christ loved us.
relevant.reason: Names another harm of riches: they hinder love of neighbour and humility.

relevant.quote: And it is no more sinful to be rich than to be poor. But it is dangerous beyond expression. Therefore, I remind all of you that are of this number, that have the conveniences of life, and something over that ye walk upon slippery ground.
relevant.reason: Direct answer: being rich is not sinful in itself, but extremely dangerous to the soul.

relevant.sermon_title: Causes of the Inefficacy of Christianity
relevant.quote: And it is an observation which admits of few exceptions, that nine in ten of these decreased in grace, in the same proportion as they increased in wealth.
relevant.reason: Wesley's observation that growing wealth usually brought declining grace.

relevant.quote: Riches have increased with thee; at the peril of thy soul, "set not thine heart upon them!" Be thankful to Him that gave thee such a talent, so much power of doing good. Yet dare not to rejoice over them, but with fear and trembling.
relevant.reason: Direct counsel to one whose riches increased: be thankful, use them for good, never set your heart on them.

relevant.reason: Wesley's remedy for the spiritual poison of wealth: spend nothing on vanity, hoard nothing, give all you can.

query: How should I pray when I am alone? What did Wesley say about private prayer?

relevant.sermon_title: Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 6
relevant.quote: But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret, he shall reward thee openly.
A direction, equally full and express, to wait for the blessings of God in private prayer, together with a positive promise, that, by this means, we shall obtain the request of our lips
relevant.reason: Wesley calls private prayer a direct command of Christ with a promise attached; answers why and that one should pray alone.

relevant.sermon_title: Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 4
relevant.quote: We have need daily to retire from the world, at least morning and evening, to converse with God, to commune more freely with our Father which is in secret.
relevant.reason: Practical counsel: withdraw daily, morning and evening, to commune with God in secret.

relevant.sermon_title: Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 6
relevant.quote: Prayer is the lifting up of the heart to God: All words of prayer, without this, are mere hypocrisy. Whenever therefore thou attemptest to pray, see that it be thy one design to commune with God
relevant.reason: Explains how to pray: sincerely lifting the heart to God, aiming only at communion with him, not at being seen.

relevant.sermon_title: Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 6
relevant.quote: Use all the privacy thou canst. (Only leave it not undone, whether thou hast any closet, any privacy, or no. Pray to God, if it be possible, when none seeth but He; but, if otherwise, pray to God.)
relevant.reason: Wesley's exposition of the closet text: seek privacy, but pray regardless; pour out your heart to the Father in secret.

relevant.sermon_title: Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 6
relevant.quote: Do not use abundance of words without any meaning. Say not the same thing over and over again; think not the fruit of your prayers depends on the length of them
relevant.reason: Direct counsel for secret prayer: avoid empty repetition and wordiness.

relevant.sermon_title: Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 6
relevant.quote: So that the end of your praying is not to inform God, as though he knew not your wants already; but rather to inform yourselves; to fix the sense of those wants more deeply in your hearts
relevant.reason: Explains what prayer is for: deepening our sense of need and dependence, readying us to receive.

relevant.sermon_title: Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 6
relevant.quote: our Lord subjoins an example of it; even that divine form of prayer which seems in this place to be proposed by way of pattern chiefly, as the model and standard of all our prayers
relevant.reason: Points the asker to the Lord's Prayer as the model for how to pray, containing all we need to ask.

relevant.quote: Perhaps no sin of omission more frequently occasions this than the neglect of private prayer; the want whereof cannot be supplied by any other ordinance whatever.
relevant.reason: Says private prayer is irreplaceable and its neglect brings spiritual darkness; strong reason to keep it.

relevant.quote: Consider both your outward and inward state, and vary your prayers accordingly.
relevant.reason: Practical advice on ordering private devotions: suit your prayers to your circumstances rather than repeating one form.

relevant.sermon_title: Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 5
relevant.quote: Are you zealous of, and diligent in, private prayer? Do you suffer no day to pass without it?
relevant.reason: Exhorts daily, unhurried private prayer and challenges those who give it little time.

query: Someone hurt me and I cannot let it go. What did Wesley say about forgiving people who wrong us?

relevant.sermon_title: Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 6
relevant.quote: For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.

relevant.sermon_title: Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 6
relevant.quote: So that if any malice or bitterness, if any taint of unkindness or anger remains, if we do not clearly, fully, and from the heart, forgive all men their trespasses, we far cut short the forgiveness of our own
relevant.reason: Explains that lingering bitterness limits God's forgiveness of us; we must forgive fully and from the heart.

relevant.sermon_title: Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 6
relevant.quote: Now, even now, by his grace, forgive as you would be forgiven! Now have compassion on thy fellow-servant, as God hath had and will have pity on thee!
relevant.reason: Direct exhortation to forgive now, by God's grace, remembering the pity God has shown you.

relevant.sermon_title: Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 3
relevant.quote: If you can do nothing more, at least "pray for them that despitefully use you and persecute you." You can never be disabled from doing this; nor can all their malice or violence hinder you.
relevant.reason: Practical counsel toward those who wrong us: pray for them always, forgive the repentant fully, wrestle with God for the unrepentant.

relevant.quote: Have you not been offended at any of your brethren, looking at their (real or imagined) sin, so as to sin yourself against the great law of love, by estranging your heart from them? Then look unto the Lord
relevant.reason: Addresses holding offence against others: it estranges the heart; look to the Lord so love returns and you forgive as God forgave.

query: What does Wesley mean by Christian perfection? Can a believer be made perfect in this life?

relevant.quote: Christian perfection, therefore, does not imply (as some men seem to have imagined) an exemption either from ignorance or mistake, or infirmities or temptations. Indeed, it is only another term for holiness.
leaving the principles of the doctrine of Christ, let us go on unto perfection
But what is perfection? The word has various senses: here it means perfect love. It is love excluding sin; love filling the heart, taking up the whole capacity of the soul.
relevant.reason: Direct definition: Christian perfection is perfect love that excludes sin and fills the whole heart.

relevant.quote: What is then the perfection of which man is capable while he dwells in a corruptible body? It is the complying with that kind command, "My son, give me thy heart."
relevant.reason: Answers what perfection is possible in this life: loving God with all the heart, summed up in love.

relevant.quote: According to this Apostle, then, perfection is another name for universal holiness: Inward and outward righteousness: Holiness of life, arising from holiness of heart.
relevant.reason: Defines Christian perfection as universal holiness of heart and life.

relevant.quote: Why cannot the Almighty sanctify the soul while it is in the body? Cannot he sanctify you while you are in this house, as well as in the open air?
relevant.reason: Argues God can save from all sin before death, and has promised it in the command to love him wholly.

relevant.quote: Believe, Fourthly, that he is not only able, but willing to do it now. Not when you come to die; not at any distant time; not to-morrow, but to-day.
relevant.reason: Says God can purify from all sin and fill the heart with love now, not at death; direct counsel to the seeker.

relevant.quote: In conformity, therefore, both to the doctrine of St. John, and to the whole tenor of the New Testament, we fix this conclusion -- A Christian is so far perfect, as not to commit sin.
relevant.reason: States in what sense a believer is perfect in this life: not committing sin, and for mature believers freedom from evil tempers.

relevant.quote: "True," say some, "we shall thus be saved from our sins; but not till death; not in this world." But how are we to reconcile this with the express words of St. John?
relevant.reason: Answers the 'only at death' objection: Scripture says believers are saved from sin in this world.

relevant.quote: It remains, then, that Christians are saved in this world from all sin, from all unrighteousness; that they are now in such a sense perfect, as not to commit sin, and to be freed from evil thoughts and evil tempers.
relevant.reason: Wesley's summary conclusion: believers can be perfect in this life, freed from sin, evil thoughts and tempers.

relevant.quote: No necessity of sinning was laid upon them. The grace of God was surely sufficient for them. And it is sufficient for us at this day.
relevant.reason: Denies that Christians must keep sinning; grace is sufficient and no one need yield to temptation.

relevant.quote: We expect to be "made perfect in love;" in that love which casts out all painful fear, and all desire but that of glorifying him we love, and of loving and serving him more and more.
relevant.reason: Describes the expected perfection in love: freedom from fear, anger, pride, and unkind tempers.

relevant.quote: But what is the "perfection" here spoken of? It is not only a deliverance from doubts and fears, but from sin; from all inward as well as outward sin
relevant.reason: Direct definition of perfection as deliverance from all inward and outward sin.

relevant.quote: Admitting, therefore, that "with men it is impossible" to "bring a clean thing out of an unclean," to purify the heart from all sin, and to till it with all holiness; yet this creates no difficulty in the case
relevant.reason: Answers 'is it possible': purifying the heart from all sin is impossible to us but possible to God.

query: What are the means of grace, and do they actually help a person grow?

relevant.quote: By "means of grace" I understand outward signs, words, or actions, ordained of God, and appointed for this end, to be the ordinary channels whereby he might convey to men, preventing, justifying, or sanctifying grace.

But we allow, that the whole value of the means depends on their actual subservience to the end of religion; that, consequently, all these means, when separate from the end, are less than nothing and vanity
relevant.reason: Names the chief means (prayer, Scripture, Supper) and says their worth lies in actually leading to the knowledge and love of God.

relevant.quote: We know that there is no inherent power in the words that are spoken in prayer, in the letter of Scripture read, the sound thereof heard, or the bread and wine received in the Lord's Supper
relevant.reason: Explains how they help: the power is God's alone, working through them, not in the practices themselves.

relevant.quote: all who desire the grace of God are to wait for it in the means which he hath ordained; in using, not in laying them aside.
relevant.reason: Wesley's central answer: those seeking God should use the means, not abandon them.

relevant.quote: And that this is a means whereby God not only gives, but also confirms and increases, true wisdom, we learn from the words of St. Paul to Timothy
relevant.reason: Says Bible reading is a means God uses to give and increase grace and wisdom; speaks to whether it helps growth.

relevant.quote: Is not the eating of that bread, and the drinking of that cup, the outward, visible means, whereby God conveys into our souls all that spiritual grace, that righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost
relevant.reason: Explains the Lord's Supper as a real channel by which God conveys grace, not an empty ritual.

relevant.quote: looking for the blessing of God therein? believing, that if I wait in this way, I shall attain what otherwise I should not? So I do. And so I will, God being my helper, even to my life's end.
relevant.reason: Wesley affirms he expects real blessing through the means because God promised it; directly answers whether they help.

relevant.quote: As to the manner of using them, whereon indeed it wholly depends whether they should convey any grace at all to the user; it behoves us, First, always to retain a lively sense, that God is above all means.
relevant.reason: Says whether the means help depends on how we use them; begins Wesley's practical rules.

relevant.quote: It is, in itself, a poor, dead, empty thing: Separate from God, it is a dry leaf, a shadow.
relevant.reason: Answers the 'just habits' worry: without God the practice is empty, but we use it because God bids and meets us there.

relevant.quote: In using all means, seek God alone. In and through every outward thing, look singly to the power of his Spirit; and the merits of his Son. Beware you do not stick in the work itself
relevant.reason: Practical counsel on keeping practices from becoming mere routine: seek God through them, use them as means.

relevant.quote: so he continued daily in all the ordinances of God, the stated channels of his grace to man
relevant.reason: Describes the early believer growing daily in grace by steadily using prayer, teaching and the Supper.

relevant.quote: God can give the end without any means at all; but you have no reason to think He will. Therefore constantly and carefully use all those means which He has appointed to be the ordinary channels of His grace.
relevant.reason: Direct counsel: do not expect growth without the appointed means; use them constantly.

relevant.quote: if a man willingly neglect them, he cannot reasonably expect that he shall ever be sanctified; he cannot grow in grace, in the image of God
relevant.reason: Says works of piety are necessary for growth; neglecting them stops growth and loses grace already given.

relevant.quote: This may be an excellent help to religion; and everyone who desires to save his soul should attend them at all opportunities; yet it is possible you may attend them all your days, and still have no religion at all.

relevant.quote: It is plain, all these fruits of love are means of increasing the love from which they spring

relevant.quote: By these we exercise all holy tempers- by these we continually improve them, so that all these are real means of grace

relevant.quote: This, then, is the foundation of the new birth, -- the entire corruption of our nature. Hence it is, that, being born in sin, we must be "born again."

relevant.quote: But as soon as he is born of God, there is a total change in all these particulars. The "eyes of his understanding are opened;"
relevant.reason: Describes the change at new birth: spiritual eyes and ears opened, hearing God say sins are forgiven.

relevant.quote: He feels, he is conscious of, a "peace which passeth all understanding." He many times feels such a joy in God as is "unspeakable, and full of glory." He feels "the love of God shed abroad in his heart
relevant.reason: Names what the born-again person inwardly experiences: peace, joy, and God's love felt in the heart.

relevant.quote: It cannot commence in the soul till that change be wrought; till, by the power of the Highest overshadowing us, we are "brought from darkness to light, from the power of Satan unto God;" that is, till we are born again
relevant.reason: Explains why the new birth is necessary: holiness, and so salvation, cannot begin without it.

relevant.quote: the one being an act of man, purifying the body; the other a change wrought by God in the soul: So that the former is just as distinguishable from the latter, as the soul from the body, or water from the Holy Ghost.
relevant.reason: Wesley's teaching that baptism is not the new birth; the new birth is God's inward change of the soul.

relevant.quote: This is a part of sanctification, not the whole; it is the gate to it, the entrance into it. When we are born again, then our sanctification, our inward and outward holiness, begins
relevant.reason: Explains new birth as the beginning of holiness, followed by gradual growth, like a child born then growing.

relevant.quote: Let this therefore, if you have not already experienced this inward work of God, be your continual prayer: "Lord, add this to all thy blessings, -- let me be born again!
relevant.reason: Direct counsel to someone who needs the new birth: church-going cannot replace it, so pray for it.

relevant.quote: In that instant we are born again, born from above, born of the Spirit: there is a real as well as a relative change. We are inwardly renewed by the power of God.
relevant.reason: Says new birth happens with justification and describes the real inward change: love replaces pride, anger, self-will.

relevant.quote: We allow, that at the very moment of justification, we are born again: In that instant we experience that inward change from "darkness into marvellous light;" from the image of the brute and the devil, into the image of God
relevant.reason: Describes the inward change at new birth, and notes it is real but not yet complete holiness.

relevant.quote: And there is as great a change wrought in our souls when we are born of the Spirit, as was wrought in our bodies when we are born of a woman. There is, in that hour, a general change from inward sinfulness, to inward holiness.
relevant.reason: Plainly states what changes when one is born of the Spirit: loves, desires, and will turned toward God.

relevant.quote: Not an outward change only, as from drunkenness to sobriety, from robbery or theft to honesty; (this is the poor, dry, miserable conceit of those that know nothing of real religion;) but an inward change from all unholy, to all holy tempers
relevant.reason: Explains the new birth as an inward change of tempers, not mere outward reform; directly answers what changes.

relevant.quote: not, on the one hand, to despise the day of small things; nor, on the other, to mistake any of these partial changes for that entire, general change, the new birth
relevant.reason: Distinguishes the new birth, a total inward change, from partial reforms people mistake for it.

relevant.quote: But when he is born of God, born of the Spirit, how is the manner of his existence changed! His whole soul is now sensible of God

It is the change wrought in the whole soul by the almighty Spirit of God when it is "created anew in Christ Jesus;" when it is "renewed after the image of God, in righteousness and true holiness;" when the love of the world is changed into the love of God; pride into humility; passion into meekness
relevant.reason: Wesley's own definition of the new birth and a list of exactly what changes inside a person.

relevant.quote: This, then, is the foundation of the new birth, -- the entire corruption of our nature. Hence it is, that, being born in sin, we must be "born again."
relevant.reason: Answers why we must be born again: our nature is corrupted from birth, so the Spirit must renew it.

relevant.quote: But as soon as he is born of God, there is a total change in all these particulars. The "eyes of his understanding are opened;"
relevant.reason: Describes the change at new birth: spiritual eyes and ears opened, hearing God say sins are forgiven.

relevant.quote: He feels, he is conscious of, a "peace which passeth all understanding." He many times feels such a joy in God as is "unspeakable, and full of glory." He feels "the love of God shed abroad in his heart
relevant.reason: Names what the born-again person inwardly experiences: peace, joy, and God's love felt in the heart.

relevant.quote: It cannot commence in the soul till that change be wrought; till, by the power of the Highest overshadowing us, we are "brought from darkness to light, from the power of Satan unto God;" that is, till we are born again
relevant.reason: Explains why the new birth is necessary: holiness, and so salvation, cannot begin without it.

relevant.quote: the one being an act of man, purifying the body; the other a change wrought by God in the soul: So that the former is just as distinguishable from the latter, as the soul from the body, or water from the Holy Ghost.
relevant.reason: Wesley's teaching that baptism is not the new birth; the new birth is God's inward change of the soul.

relevant.quote: This is a part of sanctification, not the whole; it is the gate to it, the entrance into it. When we are born again, then our sanctification, our inward and outward holiness, begins
relevant.reason: Explains new birth as the beginning of holiness, followed by gradual growth, like a child born then growing.

relevant.quote: Let this therefore, if you have not already experienced this inward work of God, be your continual prayer: "Lord, add this to all thy blessings, -- let me be born again!
relevant.reason: Direct counsel to someone who needs the new birth: church-going cannot replace it, so pray for it.

relevant.quote: In that instant we are born again, born from above, born of the Spirit: there is a real as well as a relative change. We are inwardly renewed by the power of God.
relevant.reason: Says new birth happens with justification and describes the real inward change: love replaces pride, anger, self-will.

relevant.quote: We allow, that at the very moment of justification, we are born again: In that instant we experience that inward change from "darkness into marvellous light;" from the image of the brute and the devil, into the image of God
relevant.reason: Describes the inward change at new birth, and notes it is real but not yet complete holiness.

relevant.quote: And there is as great a change wrought in our souls when we are born of the Spirit, as was wrought in our bodies when we are born of a woman. There is, in that hour, a general change from inward sinfulness, to inward holiness.
relevant.reason: Plainly states what changes when one is born of the Spirit: loves, desires, and will turned toward God.

relevant.quote: Not an outward change only, as from drunkenness to sobriety, from robbery or theft to honesty; (this is the poor, dry, miserable conceit of those that know nothing of real religion;) but an inward change from all unholy, to all holy tempers
relevant.reason: Explains the new birth as an inward change of tempers, not mere outward reform; directly answers what changes.

relevant.quote: not, on the one hand, to despise the day of small things; nor, on the other, to mistake any of these partial changes for that entire, general change, the new birth
relevant.reason: Distinguishes the new birth, a total inward change, from partial reforms people mistake for it.

relevant.quote: But when he is born of God, born of the Spirit, how is the manner of his existence changed! His whole soul is now sensible of God
relevant.reason: Describes how life changes when born of God: the soul senses God and lives by faith, love, prayer, praise.

relevant.quote: So that he who is thus justified, or saved by faith, is indeed born again. he is born again of the Spirit unto a new life, which "is hid with Christ in God."
relevant.reason: Says the one saved by faith is born again to a new life and then grows from grace to grace.

relevant.sermon_title: The Marks of the New Birth
relevant.quote: It is so to believe in God through Christ as not to commit sin and to enjoy at all times and in all places that peace of God which passeth all understanding
relevant.reason: Wesley's summary of the marks of one born of the Spirit: faith, peace, hope, the Spirit's witness, love.

relevant.sermon_title: The Marks of the New Birth
relevant.quote: An immediate and constant fruit of this faith whereby we are born of God, a fruit which can in no wise be separated from it, no, not for an hour, is power over sin
relevant.reason: Names a key change in the born-again person: power over outward and inward sin.

query: I am a Christian and I still struggle with pride and unbelief. Did Wesley say that sin remains in believers?

relevant.quote: I do not suppose any man who is justified is a slave to sin: Yet I do suppose sin remains (at least for a time) in all that are justified.
They are daily sensible of sin remaining in their heart, -- pride, self-will, unbelief; and of sin cleaving to all they speak and do
relevant.reason: Believers feel pride and unbelief yet are assured they are God's children; Christ dwells where sin remains.

relevant.quote: one says, "I felt anger to-day." Must I reply, "Then you have no faith?"
relevant.reason: Rejects telling a struggling believer he has no faith; such a doctrine wounds and disarms weak believers.

relevant.quote: Every babe in Christ is holy, and yet not altogether so. He is saved from sin; yet not entirely: It remains, though it does not reign.
relevant.reason: Direct doctrinal answer: sin remains in believers though it does not reign.

relevant.reason: Speaks to pride specifically: a believer may feel pride without being a proud man ruled by it.

relevant.quote: Resentment of an affront is sin; it is anomia, disconformity to the law of love. This has existed in me a thousand times. Yet it did not, and does not, reign.
relevant.reason: Wesley's own experience: inward sin felt but not yielded to brings no condemnation.

relevant.quote: "But how can unbelief be in a believer?" That word has two meanings. It means either no faith, or little faith; either the absence of faith or the weakness of it.
relevant.reason: Answers the doubting part: believers may have weak faith mixed with doubt without lacking faith.

relevant.quote: A man may be in God's favour though he feel sin; but not if he yields to it. Having sin does not forfeit the favour of God; giving way to sin does.
relevant.reason: Reassures that feeling sin does not mean loss of salvation; only yielding to it does.

relevant.reason: Says believers are not condemned for remaining inward sin like pride; it is daily experience.

relevant.sermon_title: THE FIRST FRUITS OF THE SPIRIT
relevant.quote: Then fret not thyself because of ungodliness, though it still remain in thy heart. Repine not, because thou still comest short of the glorious image of God; nor yet because pride, self-will, or unbelief, cleave to all thy words and works.
relevant.reason: Direct comfort to believers troubled by remaining pride and unbelief: no condemnation, do not fret.

relevant.quote: it does not reign, but it does remain. And a conviction of the sin which remains in our heart, is one great branch of the repentance we are now speaking of.
relevant.reason: Believers soon feel pride still in their hearts yet know they are in God's favour.

relevant.quote: yet they feel in themselves sometimes pride or self-will, sometimes anger or unbelief. They find one or more of these frequently stirring in their heart, though not conquering
relevant.reason: Describes the normal believer's experience of pride and unbelief stirring while still a child of God.

relevant.reason: Says sin remains in the regenerate, and recognizing it does not imply doubting God's favour.

relevant.quote: For even good men, in general, though sin has not dominion over the, yet are not freed from the remains of it. They have still the remains of an evil heart

query: How should I treat Christians who disagree with me on doctrine? What did Wesley mean by a catholic spirit?

relevant.quote: a catholic spirit is not speculative latitudinarianism. It is not an indifference to all opinions: this is the spawn of hell, not the offspring of heaven.

But although a difference in opinions or modes of worship may prevent an entire external union, yet need it prevent our union in affection? Though we cannot think alike, may we not love alike? May we not be of one heart, though we are not of one opinion? Without all doubt, we may.
relevant.reason: Direct answer: Christians who differ in opinion and worship can still be united in love and good works.

relevant.quote: Every wise man, therefore, will allow others the same liberty of thinking which he desires they should allow him; and will no more insist on their embracing his opinions, than he would have them to insist on his embracing theirs.
relevant.reason: Counsel to grant others the same freedom of judgment you want, and bear with those who differ.

relevant.quote: God has given no right to any of the children of men thus to lord it over the conscience of his brethren; but every man must judge for himself, as every man must give an account of himself to God.
relevant.reason: Explains why we must not force our views on others: each answers to God by his own conscience.

relevant.quote: Let all these things stand by: we will talk of them, if need be, at a more convenient season, my only question at present is this, "Is thine heart right, as my heart is with thy heart?"
relevant.reason: Wesley sets aside church order and sacrament disputes; the one test for fellowship is a heart right with God.

relevant.quote: Keep you your opinion; I mine; and that as steadily as ever. You need not even endeavour to come over to me, or bring me over to you.
relevant.reason: Shows how to unite without pretending: both keep their convictions firmly yet join hands in love.

relevant.quote: then love me with a very tender affection, as a friend that is closer than a brother; as a brother in Christ, a fellow citizen of the New Jerusalem, a fellow soldier engaged in the same warfare
relevant.reason: Says those who differ but whose hearts are right should be close friends and brothers in Christ.

relevant.quote: Love me so as to think no evil of me; to put away all jealousy and evil-surmising.
relevant.reason: Practical counsel on treating a fellow Christian who differs: patient love, no suspicion, best construction on their actions.

relevant.quote: commend me to God in all thy prayers; wrestle with him in my behalf, that he would speedily correct what he sees amiss, and supply what is wanting in me.
relevant.reason: Another concrete duty toward a differing Christian: pray earnestly for one another.

relevant.quote: So far as in conscience thou canst (retaining still thy own opinions, and thy own manner of worshipping God), join with me in the work of God; and let us go on hand in hand.
relevant.reason: Directly answers whether we can work together: yes, each keeping his own opinions and worship.

relevant.quote: But while he is steadily fixed in his religious principles in what he believes to be the truth as it is in Jesus; while he firmly adheres to that worship of God which he judges to be most acceptable in his sight
relevant.reason: Defines a catholic spirit: firm in one's own beliefs and church, yet loving all; catholic love is a catholic spirit.

relevant.quote: loves as friends as brethren in the Lord as members of Christ and children of God as joint partakers now of the present kingdom of God and fellow heirs of his eternal kingdom all of whatever opinion or worship or congregation who believe in the Lord Jesus Christ
relevant.reason: Wesley's fullest definition of the man of catholic spirit: keeps his own blessings, loves all believers as brethren.

relevant.quote: Take heed, lest thou be either wavering in thy judgement, or straitened in thy bowels: but keep an even pace, rooted in the faith once delivered to the saints, and grounded in love
relevant.reason: Closing exhortation: avoid both wavering convictions and narrow affections; be rooted in faith and grounded in love.

relevant.sermon_title: On the Death of the Rev. Mr. George Whitefield
relevant.quote: There are many doctrines of a less essential nature, with regard to which even the sincere children of God (such is the present weakness of human understanding) are and have been divided for many ages. In these we may think and let think; we may "agree to disagree."
relevant.reason: Counsel to agree to disagree on lesser doctrines while holding fast the essentials of the faith.

relevant.sermon_title: On the Death of the Rev. Mr. George Whitefield
relevant.quote: One who loves as friends, as brethren in the Lord, as joint partakers of the present kingdom of heaven, and fellow heirs of His eternal kingdom, all, of whatever opinion, mode of worship, or congregation, who believe in the Lord Jesus
relevant.reason: Answers who is the man of a catholic spirit: he loves, prays for, and helps believers of every persuasion.

relevant.sermon_title: On the Death of the Rev. Mr. George Whitefield
relevant.quote: Go and learn that truly catholic love which "is not rash," or hasty in judging; that love which "thinks no evil;" which "believes and hopes all things;" which makes all the allowances for others that we desire others should make for us!
relevant.reason: Exhorts to catholic love that judges slowly and sees God's grace in others whatever their opinion or worship.

relevant.quote: I say seem; because I am throughly convinced, that many of them only seem to differ. The disagreement is more in words than in sentiments: They are much nearer in judgment than in language.
relevant.reason: Points out that many doctrinal disagreements among believers are more in words than in substance.

relevant.quote: How then can we be rigorous in requiring others to use just the same expressions with us? 3. We may go a step farther yet: Men may differ from us in their opinions, as well as their expressions, and nevertheless be partakers with us of the same precious faith.
relevant.reason: Says those who differ in expression or even opinion may share the same saving faith; don't demand uniformity.

relevant.quote: Bear with me, as I do with you; else how shall we "fulfil the law of Christ?"
relevant.reason: Wesley's own plea to a doctrinal opponent: bear with each other, same foundation, no coldness or unkindness.

relevant.quote: If he forbid you, do not you forbid him. Rather labour, and watch, and pray the more, to confirm your love toward him. If he speak all manner of evil of you, speak all manner of good (that is true) of him.
relevant.reason: Counsel for when a Christian of another party opposes you: do not retaliate, increase your love and speak well.

relevant.quote: Do I not discourage him, because he is not of my Church, by disputing with him concerning it, by raising objections, and by perplexing his mind with distant consequences?

relevant.quote: Whoever they are that have one Spirit one hope one Lord one faith one God and Father of all I can easily bear with their holding wrong opinions yea and superstitious modes of worship
relevant.reason: Wesley bears with those holding wrong opinions if they share one Spirit, Lord, and faith.

query: What does it mean to deny yourself and take up your cross? What did Wesley say about self-denial?

relevant.quote: The denying ourselves and the taking up our cross, in the full extent of the expression, is not a thing of small concern: It is not expedient only, as are some of the circumstantials of religion; but it is absolutely, indispensably necessary, either to our becoming or continuing his disciples.
We see the nature of self-denial: It is the denying or refusing to follow ours own will, from a conviction that the will of God is the only rule of action to us.
relevant.reason: Wesley's definition of self-denial and its ground: refusing our own will because God's will is our only rule.

relevant.quote: He cannot, at one and the same time, follow his own will, and follow the will of God: He must choose the one or the other; denying God's will, to follow his own; or denying himself, to follow the will of God.
relevant.reason: Explains why self-denial is unavoidable: our will and God's now run in opposite directions, so we must choose.

relevant.quote: to deny ourselves, is, to deny our own will, where it does not fall in with the will of God; and that however pleasing it may be. It is, to deny ourselves any pleasure which does not spring from, and lead to, God
relevant.reason: Answers how much to give up: any pleasure or wish not in line with God's will; also defines the cross.

relevant.quote: it is often needful to pluck out, as it were, a right eye, to cut off a right hand; -- so painful is either the thing itself which must be done, or the only means of doing it; the parting, suppose, with a foolish desire, with an inordinate affection
relevant.reason: Says following Christ may mean painfully parting with a cherished desire or attachment, to heal the soul.

relevant.quote: So when our Lord said to the rich young man, "Go, sell that thou hast, and give it to the poor," (as well knowing, this was the only means of healing his covetousness,) the very thought of it gave him so much pain, that "he went away sorrowful;"
relevant.reason: Uses the rich young ruler to show a cross Christ may ask: giving up what we cling to.

relevant.quote: we do not properly "take up our cross," but when we voluntarily suffer what it is in our power to avoid; when we willingly embrace the will of God, though contrary to our own
relevant.reason: Explains what taking up the cross means, as distinct from bearing what is imposed: freely embracing God's will.

relevant.quote: In all this, we may easily conceive our blessed Lord to act as the Physician of our souls, not merely "for his own pleasure, but for our profit, that we may be partakers of his holiness."
relevant.reason: Reassures that the cross God gives is measured for our good, like a physician causing pain only to heal.

relevant.quote: It does not imply the disciplining ourselves; (as some speak;) the literally tearing our own flesh: the wearing hair-cloth, or iron-girdles, or anything else that would impair our bodily health
relevant.reason: Clarifies what self-denial is not (self-torment) and what it is: embracing God's will even when painful.

relevant.quote: But where none of these is wanting, the great hindrance of our receiving or growing in the grace of God is always the want of denying ourselves, or taking up our cross.
relevant.reason: Explains why self-denial matters: lack of it is always the main hindrance to receiving or growing in grace.

relevant.quote: Delay not the time, but practise it immediately, from this very hour! Practise it universally, on every one of the thousand occasions which will occur in all circumstances of life! Practise it daily
relevant.reason: Direct exhortation on how to practise self-denial: now, in everyday particulars, daily, asking God for strength.

relevant.quote: unless a man do "deny himself" every pleasure which does not prepare him for taking pleasure in God, "and take up his cross daily,"--obey every command of God, however grievous to flesh and blood,--he cannot be a disciple of Christ
relevant.reason: States the measure of self-denial: give up any pleasure that doesn't lead to delight in God; obey even when hard.

query: My mind wanders when I try to pray. Are wandering thoughts a sin? What did Wesley say?

The imagination, without leave, starts to and fro, and carries us away hither and thither, whether we will or no; and all this from the merely natural motion of the spirits, or vibration of the nerves.

relevant.reason: Answers which wandering thoughts are sinful: those that wander from God himself, not mere distraction.

relevant.reason: Distinguishes when innocent distractions become sin: only when they feed a wrong desire or temper.

relevant.quote: It follows that none of these wandering thoughts (whatever unwary persons have affirmed, thereby grieving whom the Lord had not grieved) are inconsistent with perfect love.

relevant.quote: those wherein the heart wanders from God; from all that are contrary to his will, or that leave us without God in the world; every one that is perfected in love is unquestionably delivered.

query: I used to feel close to God, and now everything feels dark. What did Wesley say about the wilderness state?

relevant.quote: some, in allusion to the case of the Israelites, have termed "a wilderness state."

It properly consists in the loss of that faith which God once wrought in their heart. They that are in the wilderness, have not now that divine "evidence," that satisfactory conviction "of things not seen," which they once enjoyed.
relevant.reason: Defines the wilderness state: loss of the clear faith and sense of God the believer once had.

relevant.quote: In consequence of the loss of faith and love, follows, Thirdly, loss of joy in the Holy Ghost. For if the loving consciousness of pardon be no more, the joy resulting therefrom cannot remain.
relevant.reason: Explains why the former joy has gone: it flowed from a faith and witness that have weakened.

relevant.quote: That sweet tranquillity of mind, that composure of spirit, is gone. Painful doubt returns; doubt, whether we ever did, and perhaps whether we ever shall, believe.
relevant.reason: Describes the lost peace and the doubts about whether one ever truly believed, a symptom the asker may feel.

relevant.quote: Therefore he never deserts us, as some speak; it is we only that desert him. (I.) 2. The most usual cause of inward darkness is sin, of one kind or another.
relevant.reason: Answers 'what happened': God does not arbitrarily withdraw; darkness most often comes from sin.

relevant.quote: If therefore we are negligent of this, if we suffer business, company, or any avocation whatever, to prevent these secret exercises of the soul
relevant.reason: Names neglect of private prayer as a common cause of the soul's life gradually dying away.

relevant.quote: And if we will not hear his warning voice, and return to him with our whole soul, we continue to grieve him with our idols, and running after other gods, we shall soon be cold, barren, and dry
relevant.reason: Explains how desiring things other than God leaves a believer cold, barren and dry.

relevant.quote: Let us only be careless or "faint in our mind," let us be easy and indolent, and our natural darkness will soon return, and overspread our soul.

relevant.quote: Now, when so various assaults are made at once, and perhaps with the utmost violence, it is not strange if it should occasion, not only heaviness, but even darkness in a weak believer

relevant.quote: Whereas, indeed, the cure of spiritual, as of bodily diseases, must be as various as are the causes of them. The first thing, therefore, is to find out the cause; and this will naturally point out the cure.

relevant.quote: And how can you expect they should return, till you put away the accursed thing?
relevant.reason: Direct counsel: if sin drove away joy and peace, forsake it and the Lord will return and pardon.

relevant.quote: It is vain to hope for a recovery of his light, till you pluck out the right eye, and cast it from you. O let there be no longer delay! Cry to Him, that he may enable you so to do!

relevant.quote: Arise, and shake yourself from the dust; wrestle with God for the mighty blessing; pour out your soul unto God in prayer, and continue therein with all perseverance!

query: My company is replacing people with AI and I might not have a job next year. How do I stop panicking?

relevant.sermon_title: Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 9
relevant.quote: Take no uneasy thought: This is a plain, sure rule, Uneasy care is unlawful care. With a single eye to God, do all that in you lies to provide things honest in the sight of all men. And then give up all into better hands; leave the whole event to God.
relevant.reason: Direct counsel for job worry: do all you can to provide, then leave the outcome to God instead of fretting.

relevant.sermon_title: Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 9
relevant.quote: It is good and acceptable to God, that we should so take thought concerning whatever we have in hand, as to have a clear comprehension of what we are about to do, and to plan our business before we enter upon it.
relevant.reason: Says sensible planning pleases God; preparing for a possible job loss is right, unlike the anxious care he forbids.

relevant.sermon_title: Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 9
relevant.quote: Why should you perplex yourself without need? God provides for you to-day what is needful to sustain the life which he hath given you. It is enough: Give yourself up into his hands. If you live another day, he will provide for that also.
relevant.reason: Tells the anxious not to dwell on next year: God provides for today and will provide for tomorrow.

relevant.sermon_title: Upon our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, Discourse 9
relevant.quote: This care God hath taken upon himself: Cast you all your care upon Him. He knoweth your wants; and whatsoever is lacking he will not fail to supply.
relevant.reason: Promise for one fearing loss of income: God knows your needs and will supply what is lacking; cast your care on him.

relevant.quote: Thou shalt not; thou canst not: It is absolutely impossible, unless God himself chooseth it; for his "kingdom ruleth over all," and "the very hairs of thy head are all numbered."
relevant.reason: Answers fear of losing one's livelihood: it cannot happen unless God chooses it, and he numbers every hair.
